questions.question: What is a personal budget?
choices: A record of a company's stock price only
A guarantee that expenses will never change
A plan for income, spending, and saving
A statement showing only money borrowed

questions.question: What is gross pay?
choices: Earnings before taxes and other deductions
Take-home earnings after all deductions
Only money placed in savings
Only an employer's benefit expenses

questions.question: What is net pay?
choices: Pay before deductions
Pay remaining after deductions
The total value of a household's property
The amount borrowed on a credit card

questions.question: Which expense is commonly fixed over a short budgeting period?
choices: Grocery purchases that vary each week
Fuel purchases that change with travel
Restaurant spending that depends on choices
A lease's stated monthly rent

questions.question: Which expense is typically variable?
choices: Grocery spending
A fixed lease payment
A fixed monthly loan installment
A subscription with an unchanged monthly price

questions.question: What is a budget deficit for a household over a period?
choices: Income exceeds all planned outflows
Income and outflows are equal
Planned outflows exceed income
Every expense is classified as fixed

questions.question: What is an emergency fund intended to support?
choices: Only planned luxury purchases
Unexpected necessary expenses or interruptions in income
Speculation on daily stock movements
Payments that can never vary

questions.question: Why should a budget usually be based on take-home pay?
choices: Gross pay always equals available cash
Deductions are paid back automatically each month
Taxes affect only businesses
That is the income available after payroll deductions

questions.question: Why should irregular expenses be included in planning?
choices: Costs may be due later even without a payment this month
Annual bills should count only if they occur every month
Only fixed monthly expenses affect the household's available income
Future expenses can be ignored until the exact due date

questions.question: How can tracking actual spending improve a budget?
choices: It guarantees that every future expense disappears
It changes all variable expenses into fixed ones
It reveals differences between the plan and real transactions
It replaces the need to record income

questions.question: Why should a savings goal include an amount and deadline?
choices: They guarantee a higher interest rate
They help determine how much must be set aside over time
They eliminate the need to consider income
They make all spending choices identical

questions.question: How does cash-flow timing differ from a monthly total?
choices: Timing measures only a household's total net worth
A positive monthly total guarantees enough cash every day
Timing is unrelated to pay dates
Timing concerns when money arrives and bills must be paid

questions.question: Why can a realistic budget change over time?
choices: Income, prices, obligations, and goals may change
Every budget must remain unchanged permanently
Only people with no income can revise budgets
Past spending determines all future expenses exactly

questions.question: How can identifying needs and wants support budgeting?
choices: It proves that every preference is legally required
It makes all households' priorities identical
It helps prioritize spending when resources are limited
It removes every trade-off from spending

questions.question: Why should debt payments appear in a budget?
choices: Repayment never affects cash flow
They are obligations that use available cash
Only new purchases require budgeting
Debt payments automatically count as wages

questions.question: A student takes home $1,200 and plans $950 in expenses and $150 in savings. What remains unallocated?
A household plans for a $600 annual bill by saving equal amounts monthly. What monthly amount is needed?
A goal requires $900 in six months with no interest. What equal monthly saving meets it?
Income arrives on the 15th, but a bill is due on the 10th. What issue must the budget address?
choices: Only the annual income total
Cash-flow timing and funds carried from earlier periods
Only the household's home value
Only the interest rate on unrelated investments

questions.question: A household's spending exceeds income by $80 monthly. Which change closes that gap, with other amounts unchanged?
choices: Reduce spending by $20 while leaving income unchanged
Move the same expenses to different categories
Record the deficit as earned income
Reduce spending or increase net income by $80
